title: The Risalah
hookLine: his book laid out the method of law, founding usul al-fiqh

cards: A hadith scholar in Basra, Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi, writes to al-Shafi'i with a request, as the story is told: write me something on how the Qur'an is to be understood, on when a report is to be accepted, on consensus, and on how one text can replace another.
Explain how it all fits. Al-Shafi'i answers, and the answer grows into a book. It keeps the plain name of what it was: al-Risalah, the letter.
With it, scholars had a shared page on which to argue over method, not only over rulings.

teach.h: USUL AL-FIQH: THE ROOTS OF LAW.
teach.b: These last two weeks showed Kufa's careful judgment and Medina's living practice, each strong, each sure of itself. Al-Shafi'i asked something prior: before any ruling, how do we know where to look, and in what order?
That's usul al-fiqh, the roots of law, and tradition remembers the Risalah as the book where that discipline begins. The order he set: the Qur'an first.
Then the sunnah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, which al-Shafi'i argued explains the Qur'an and must be followed, even when it comes through a single reliable narrator.
That pushed against Medina's practice, where the city could outweigh a lone report. Then consensus. Then analogy, qiyas, measured carefully from a text.
Then a method for language. A verse can sound general and still be meant more narrowly. One text can explain another.

teach.h: TWO REPORTS CLASH: SEEK BOTH TRUE.
teach.b: When two reports seem to clash, his first move is to look for a way both are true before setting either aside.
And the argument from Abu Hanifa's school: in the Risalah he rejects istihsan where it isn't tied to a text, calling it a jurist pleasing himself. The Hanafis kept arguing back.

teach.h: WHAT IS YOUR SOURCE, YOUR STEP?
teach.b: Some readers say that even then, the argument ran in his terms: what is your source, and what is your step? Not the answer first. Method first.

how: Students of Islamic law study usul al-fiqh, the roots of law, alongside the rulings themselves, and al-Shafi'i's Risalah is read as a foundational work in that field.

o: Malik's book of law, arranged by topic and read in Spain
al-Shafi'i's letter that grew into a book on legal method

p: a specific text narrows a general one

s: the Risalah began as a list of rulings
it began as a letter answering how law is to be found: sources, order, method.
al-Shafi'i argued that a reliable report from a single narrator must be followed
it explains the Qur'an, he said, even when one reliable person carries it.
when two reports seem to clash, al-Shafi'i drops the weaker one at once
his first move is to look for a way both are true.

games.q: you're al-Shafi'i. two sound reports seem to say opposite things. what's your first move?
o: pick the one that suits the case.
set both aside and use your own judgment.
look for a way both can be true.
games.why: reconcile first. only if that fails does he ask whether one replaced the other, or weigh them.

practice: Here's one principle al-Shafi'i works through: the Qur'an gives children shares in their parents' estate in general terms, a report in Jami' al-Tirmidhi says a killer does not inherit, and the general rule stands while the specific one narrows it.

Now take a broad rule you keep, like always answering the phone for family, and name a specific exception you already live by. Notice how the two fit together instead of fighting, and if you pray, ask for clear understanding.

wordCard.voice: The Risalah. Al-Shafi'i's letter that grew into a book, setting out how law is to be found: its sources, their order, and how texts explain each other. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the letter, the message; the name of al-Shafi'i's book on method.

carryVoice: Your line: method first. Before you argue over an answer, ask where to look. Until tomorrow.
